tf.statement: Two learning procedures that both produce a linear class boundary must estimate their parameters by the same statistical objective.
tf.explanation: Gaussian LDA estimates class-conditional distributions and priors, whereas logistic regression optimizes a conditional Bernoulli likelihood. The same form of boundary does not identify the training objective.

tf.statement: For any fixed \(w\) and \(w_0\), the set \(\{x:w^{\mathsf T}x+w_0=0\}\) is a separating hyperplane of dimension \(d-1\).
tf.explanation: This requires \(w\ne0\). If \(w=0\), the zero set is either the whole space or empty, depending on the intercept.

tf.statement: Multiplying both the weights and intercept of a binary linear score by a positive constant preserves the predicted labels but generally changes its sigmoid probabilities.
tf.explanation: The score sign is unchanged; sigmoid is strictly monotone but not invariant to multiplication of its argument. Classification geometry and probability calibration have different scale behavior.

tf.statement: A multiclass argmax classifier with affine scores can have a nonconvex class region even when there are no ties.
tf.explanation: Each class region is an intersection of score-comparison half-spaces and is convex. This statement concerns affine-score argmax, not arbitrary voting combinations.

tf.statement: When training a one-vs.-one classifier for classes \(C_i\) and \(C_j\), examples from other classes are excluded from that particular binary training problem.
tf.explanation: The pairwise score constrains the relative classes only; samples from a third class have no required sign for this subproblem.

tf.statement: Training \(K\) independent one-vs.-rest sigmoid models automatically makes their \(K\) outputs sum to one.
tf.explanation: Independent sigmoids do not share a denominator. Softmax imposes a joint normalization across all classes; independent binary probabilities need not sum to one.

tf.statement: A standard linear logistic-regression model requires every input feature to have a Gaussian class-conditional distribution.
tf.explanation: The assumed affine quantity is the conditional log-odds. Gaussian shared-covariance distributions imply such a model, but they are not necessary to fit it; discrete features are allowed.

tf.statement: For finite binary logits and no numerical rounding, sigmoid produces probabilities strictly between zero and one.
tf.explanation: For finite real \(a\), both the exponential and the denominator are positive, and \(0<1/(1+e^{-a})<1\). Values zero or one are limits rather than finite-logit outputs.

tf.statement: Convexity of unregularized logistic cross-entropy guarantees a finite maximum-likelihood parameter vector on every strictly linearly separable dataset.
tf.explanation: Along a separating direction the parameter norm can diverge while cross-entropy decreases toward zero without attaining zero at any finite vector. Convexity does not ensure attainment.

tf.statement: The batch algorithm shown in the lecture accumulates errors over all samples before updating the weight vector.
tf.explanation: The parameter update is outside the full sample loop. Updating after each sample would be a different, sequential optimization procedure.

tf.statement: Adding the same input-dependent affine function to every softmax class score leaves every predicted class probability unchanged.
tf.explanation: The common exponential factor cancels from numerator and denominator at each input. This also creates parameter non-identifiability in the symmetric parameterization.

tf.statement: For one-hot softmax cross-entropy, a sample generally contributes a gradient to the weights of classes other than its true class.
tf.explanation: For a nontrue class \(j\), the error is \(y_j-0\), generally nonzero because its score competes in the shared normalization.

mc.stem: Let \(w=(4,-3)^{\mathsf T}\), \(w_0=-5\), and \(x=(2,0)^{\mathsf T}\). Which statements are correct?

options.text: The score at \(x\) equals three.
The Euclidean distance from \(x\) to the boundary equals three.
options.why: The score must be divided by \(\|w\|=5\), giving distance \(3/5\).

options.text: The orthogonal projection is \((38/25,9/25)^{\mathsf T}\).
options.why: Subtract \((3/25)(4,-3)^{\mathsf T}\) from \((2,0)^{\mathsf T}\).

options.text: The ordinary distance from the origin to the boundary equals minus one.
options.why: Ordinary distance is nonnegative; its value is \(|-5|/5=1\).

mc.stem: Three independently trained affine scores at one test point are \((-2,-1,-3)\). The specified decision rule is argmax over these scores, with no rejection option. Which statements are correct?

options.text: The predicted class is \(C_2\).
options.why: Minus one is the largest of the three scores. Scores need not be positive to win an argmax.

options.text: The point must be rejected because every score is negative.
options.why: The specified rule chooses the largest score and includes no reject action.

options.text: No label can be assigned until the scores have been individually transformed to probabilities.
options.why: Argmax on the raw scores is already a fully specified classification rule.

options.text: Adding ten to every score changes the argmax class.
options.why: A common shift preserves all pairwise score differences.

mc.stem: Consider \(g(x)=x_1^2+x_2^2-1\), with \(C_1\) predicted for \(g(x)>0\). Which statements are correct?

options.text: The boundary is a unit circle in the original input plane.
options.why: The zero set is \(x_1^2+x_2^2=1\).

options.text: The score is affine in the transformed feature \(z=x_1^2+x_2^2\).
options.why: It becomes \(g=z-1\), an affine function of the new feature.

options.text: The boundary is a straight line in the original input plane because the coefficients enter linearly.
options.why: Linearity in coefficients does not force a linear boundary in the original input.

options.text: The model requires \(x\) to have a Gaussian distribution.
options.why: A fixed basis-function discriminant does not itself impose Gaussian input densities.

mc.stem: A binary logistic model predicts \(y=1/4\) for a sample with label \(r=1\) and feature vector \(x=(1,-2)^{\mathsf T}\). Which statements are correct?

options.text: The sample cross-entropy is \(\log4\).
options.why: For a positive label, the loss is \(-\log y\).

options.text: The intercept gradient is \(-3/4\).
options.why: It equals \(y-r=1/4-1\).

options.text: The feature-weight gradient is \((-3/4,-3/2)^{\mathsf T}\).
options.why: Multiply the error \(-3/4\) by each feature; the second entry is \(+3/2\).

options.text: The negative-gradient update decreases the intercept when the learning rate is positive.
options.why: The gradient is negative, so a descent step increases the intercept.
The odds are nine, so the probability is \(9/(1+9)\).

options.text: The largest derivative value is \(1/4\), attained at \(a=0\).
options.why: \(\sigma'(a)=\sigma(a)(1-\sigma(a))\) is maximized at probability \(1/2\).

options.text: The derivative equals zero at every finite positive logit.
options.why: The derivative is strictly positive for every finite logit.

options.text: \(\sigma(a+b)=\sigma(a)+\sigma(b)\) for all real \(a,b\).
options.why: For example, take both arguments zero: the two sides are \(1/2\) and one.

mc.stem: Correct decisions cost zero. Predicting \(C_1\) when the truth is \(C_2\) costs three; the reverse error costs two. At a point with \(y=P(C_1\mid x)=0.55\), which statements are correct?

options.text: The risk-minimizing rule predicts \(C_1\) when \(y>3/5\).
options.why: Compare \(3(1-y)\) against \(2y\).

options.text: The rule must predict \(C_1\) at the given point because \(0.55>0.5\).
options.why: The cost-sensitive threshold is \(0.6\); at this point \(C_2\) has lower risk.

options.text: The risk of predicting \(C_2\) at the point is \(0.9\).
The equivalent logit threshold is \(\log(2/3)\).
options.why: The threshold is \(\log((3/5)/(2/5))=\log(3/2)\).

mc.source: PDF pp.24,30; supplementary application of lecture 05 loss rule

mc.stem: Three softmax logits are \((0,\log3,\log2)\). Which statements are correct?

options.text: The second class has probability \(1/2\).
options.why: The exponentials are \((1,3,2)\), whose sum is six.

options.text: Adding seven to every logit preserves all three probabilities.
options.why: The same exponential factor cancels from the softmax.

options.text: The posterior odds of \(C_2\) against \(C_3\) equal \(3/2\).
options.why: The common denominator cancels in the probability ratio.

options.text: The predicted class must be rejected because its probability does not strictly exceed \(1/2\).
options.why: Multiclass argmax needs no universal \(1/2\) threshold; rejection requires a separately specified rule.

mc.stem: At a point where softmax probabilities are \((0.2,0.5,0.3)\), which statements are correct?

options.text: \(\partial y_2/\partial a_1=-0.1\).
options.why: For different indices the derivative is \(-y_2y_1\).

options.text: \(\partial y_2/\partial a_2=0.5\).
options.why: The derivative is \(0.5(1-0.5)=0.25\).

options.text: The Jacobian is diagonal because each numerator uses one score.
options.why: The common denominator gives off-diagonal derivatives \(-y_i y_j\).

options.text: Every column of the Jacobian sums to one.
options.why: Every column sums to zero, since the total probability is the constant one.

mc.stem: Let a batch contain four samples. Compare summed cross-entropy and average cross-entropy at exactly the same weights. Which statements are correct?

options.text: At the same learning rate, the average-loss gradient step is one quarter of the summed-loss step.
options.why: Averaging divides the full gradient by four.

options.text: Choosing the average-loss learning rate four times as large reproduces the summed-loss update.
options.why: Then the scale factor in the learning rate cancels the factor \(1/4\) in the gradient.

options.text: Updating weights after every sample is necessarily identical to accumulating the four gradients at fixed weights.
options.why: Sequential updates evaluate later gradients at changed weights.

options.text: Zero initialization forces the binary logistic gradient to be zero for every labeled dataset.
options.why: Initial predictions are \(1/2\), but the weighted label residuals generally do not cancel.

mc.stem: Two Gaussian classes have means \(1\) and \(-1\), shared variance two, and equal priors. Which statements are correct?

options.text: The posterior probability of \(C_1\) is \(\sigma(x)\).
options.why: The logit slope is \((1-(-1))/2=1\), and the intercept is zero.

options.text: Changing only the priors, with means and variance fixed, changes only the logit intercept.
options.why: The prior contribution is the additive log prior ratio.

options.text: This derivation proves that all logistic input distributions must be Gaussian.
options.why: It shows sufficiency of a shared-covariance Gaussian model, not necessity.

options.text: Two distinct Gaussian variances always yield the same linear logit.
options.why: An unequal-variance log density ratio generally retains a quadratic term.

mc.stem: Consider adding \(\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2/2\), with \(\lambda>0\), to a finite-sample linear binary logistic loss, where \(\theta\) includes the intercept. Which statements are correct?

options.text: The added Hessian is \(\lambda I\).
options.why: The gradient of the full quadratic penalty is \(\lambda\theta\).

options.text: The penalized objective has a unique finite minimizer.
options.why: The positive quadratic penalty is coercive and makes the convex loss strongly convex.

options.text: The penalty necessarily sets some fitted coefficients exactly to zero.
options.why: L2 shrinkage does not in general produce exact sparsity.

options.text: The penalty weight can be selected using validation data.
options.why: This is a model-selection choice; the final test set should remain independent.

mc.source: PDF p.37; supplementary connection to regularization

mc.stem: A four-class softmax model has two original input features and an intercept per class. Which statements are correct?

options.text: The symmetric parameterization has twelve coefficients.
options.why: There are four rows, each with three coefficients.

options.text: Fixing the reference-class score to zero leaves nine free coefficients.
options.why: Three remaining classes each need two weights and one intercept.

options.text: Adding the same three-component augmented weight vector to every class changes the probabilities.
options.why: It adds a common affine score, which cancels.

options.text: For a row-weight matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{4\times3}\), the gradient has the same \(4\times3\) shape.
options.why: With sample rows, it is \((Y-R)^{\mathsf T}\widetilde X\).

mc.source: PDF pp.38-44; supplementary matrix and identifiability notation

long.title: Derive the geometry rather than treating the score as a distance
long.source: PDF pp.11-15; supplementary projection and scale proof

parts.question: Let \(g(x)=w^{\mathsf T}x+b\), with \(w\ne0\). Prove that \(w\) is normal to its zero hyperplane by comparing two points on that hyperplane.
parts.solution: For boundary points \(u,v\), subtract \(w^{\mathsf T}u+b=0\) and \(w^{\mathsf T}v+b=0\). This gives \(w^{\mathsf T}(u-v)=0\). Every displacement within the affine hyperplane is of this form, so \(w\) is perpendicular to it.

parts.question: Write a point as \(x=x_p+r w/\|w\|_2\), where \(x_p\) is its orthogonal projection. Derive both the signed-distance formula and an explicit formula for \(x_p\). Explain the corresponding unsigned distance.
parts.solution: Substitution gives \(g(x)=g(x_p)+r w^{\mathsf T}w/\|w\|_2=r\|w\|_2\). Hence \(r=g(x)/\|w\|_2\), and rearranging the decomposition gives \[x_p=x-\frac{w^{\mathsf T}x+b}{\|w\|_2^2}w.\] The ordinary distance is \(|r|\), not \(r\). Substituting the projection in the boundary equation yields zero and verifies the formula.

parts.question: Prove what happens to the hyperplane, signed distance, and predicted class when \((w,b)\) is multiplied by \(c>0\). Does the corresponding sigmoid probability remain fixed? Include the degenerate case \(w=0\).
parts.solution: The new score is \(cg(x)\), so its zero set and sign are unchanged. Its norm is \(c\|w\|\), so \(cg(x)/(c\|w\|)=g(x)/\|w\|\). The probability becomes \(\sigma(cg(x))\), generally different when \(c\ne1\) and \(g(x)\ne0\). If \(w=0\), the score is constant and the zero set is all of space when \(b=0\), or empty otherwise; the distance formula is undefined.

long.title: Derive the LDA-to-logistic bridge with its assumptions

parts.question: Assume \(x\mid C_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu_i,\Sigma)\) for two classes, with shared positive-definite \(\Sigma\) and positive priors \(\pi_i\). Derive \(\log[P(C_1\mid x)/P(C_2\mid x)]=w^{\mathsf T}x+b\), explicitly finding \(w,b\).
parts.solution: Bayes rule cancels the common evidence. The Gaussian normalizers also cancel because covariance is shared. Expanding both quadratic exponents gives \[\log\frac{P(C_1\mid x)}{P(C_2\mid x)}=(\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}x-\frac12(\mu_1^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_1-\mu_2^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_2)+\log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_2}.\] The common \(x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}x\) cancels and symmetry combines the cross terms. Thus \(w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\) and \(b=-\tfrac12(\mu_1^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_1-\mu_2^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_2)+\log(\pi_1/\pi_2)\).

parts.question: Solve \(a=\log[y/(1-y)]\) for \(y\), and prove the equivalence between the equal-cost posterior threshold and the zero-score threshold.
parts.solution: Exponentiating gives \(e^a(1-y)=y\), so \(y=e^a/(1+e^a)=\sigma(a)\). Since sigmoid is increasing and \(\sigma(0)=1/2\), \(y>1/2\) is equivalent to \(a>0\).

parts.question: Identify the canceled term that generally remains with unequal class covariances. Explain why the Gaussian derivation does not impose a Gaussian-input requirement on discriminatively fitted logistic regression.
parts.solution: With unequal covariances, the difference contains \(-\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}(\Sigma_1^{-1}-\Sigma_2^{-1})x\), generally quadratic. Shared Gaussian covariances are a sufficient generative explanation of affine posterior log-odds. Logistic regression instead assumes that conditional log-odds are affine and fits the conditional label likelihood directly, without requiring Gaussian class densities.

long.title: Derive Bernoulli cross-entropy, its gradient, and its limits
long.source: PDF pp.31-37; supplementary Hessian and nonattainment proof

parts.question: For conditionally independent labels \(r^t\in\{0,1\}\) with \(y^t=\sigma(\theta^{\mathsf T}\widetilde x^t)\), derive the conditional likelihood and its negative log-likelihood. Here \(\widetilde x^t\) contains the intercept feature.
parts.solution: Each label has probability \((y^t)^{r^t}(1-y^t)^{1-r^t}\). Conditional independence gives \[L(\theta)=\prod_t(y^t)^{r^t}(1-y^t)^{1-r^t},\quad E(\theta)=-\sum_t[r^t\log y^t+(1-r^t)\log(1-y^t)].\] This is binary cross-entropy; the inputs are held fixed during conditional fitting.

parts.question: Use the chain rule to derive \(\nabla_\theta E=\sum_t(y^t-r^t)\widetilde x^t\). Then derive the Hessian and prove convexity without treating sigmoid itself as a linear function.
parts.solution: For one sample, \(dy/da=y(1-y)\) and \(\partial\ell/\partial y=-r/y+(1-r)/(1-y)\). Their product is \(-r(1-y)+(1-r)y=y-r\). Because \(\partial a/\partial\theta=\widetilde x\), summation gives the gradient. Differentiating again yields \[H=\sum_t y^t(1-y^t)\widetilde x^t(\widetilde x^t)^{\mathsf T}.\] For any \(v\), \(v^{\mathsf T}Hv=\sum_t y^t(1-y^t)(v^{\mathsf T}\widetilde x^t)^2\ge0\), establishing convexity. The descent increment is minus this gradient.

parts.question: For the two observations \((x,r)=(-2,0),(2,1)\), set intercept zero and slope \(c>0\). Prove that the unregularized minimum need not be attained at a finite parameter, although the classification error is already zero.
parts.solution: Both samples have correct-label probability \(\sigma(2c)\), so \(E(c)=2\log(1+e^{-2c})\). This is positive for finite \(c\) and tends to zero as \(c\to\infty\). For every \(c>0\) both labels are correct. Thus the infimum is zero, with no finite minimizing slope along this perfectly separating dataset.

long.title: Derive softmax normalization and the coupled learning rule

parts.question: Take \(C_K\) as reference and assume \(\log[P(C_i\mid x)/P(C_K\mid x)]=a_i\) for \(i<K\). Derive all class probabilities from normalization, then express them in symmetric softmax form.
parts.solution: Exponentiating yields \(P_i=e^{a_i}P_K\). Summing probabilities gives \(1=P_K[1+\sum_{i<K}e^{a_i}]\). Therefore \(P_K=[1+\sum_{i<K}e^{a_i}]^{-1}\) and \(P_i=e^{a_i}/[1+\sum_{j<K}e^{a_j}]\). This is softmax with reference score zero. Adding a common score to every class yields the symmetric form \(y_i=e^{a_i}/\sum_j e^{a_j}\).

parts.question: Derive \(\partial y_i/\partial a_j\), then derive \(\partial\ell/\partial a_j=y_j-r_j\) for one-hot cross-entropy. Give feature-weight and intercept gradients for affine scores.
parts.solution: Let \(Z=\sum_k e^{a_k}\). The quotient rule gives \(\partial y_i/\partial a_j=(\delta_{ij}e^{a_i}Z-e^{a_i}e^{a_j})/Z^2=y_i(\delta_{ij}-y_j)\). Then \[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial a_j}=-\sum_i\frac{r_i}{y_i}y_i(\delta_{ij}-y_j)=-r_j+y_j\sum_i r_i=y_j-r_j.\] This uses \(\sum_i r_i=1\). Thus \(\partial\ell/\partial w_{j0}=y_j-r_j\) and \(\nabla_{w_j}\ell=(y_j-r_j)x\), with sums over samples for the full loss.

parts.question: Prove softmax invariance to a common affine score shift, give the free parameter count after fixing a reference class, and explain why a nontrue class still receives a gradient.
parts.solution: Adding \(c(x)\) multiplies every numerator and the denominator by \(e^{c(x)}\), which cancels. For \(K\) classes with \(d\) features and intercepts, fixing one class score to zero leaves \((K-1)(d+1)\) free coefficients instead of the redundant \(K(d+1)\). A nontrue class has \(r_j=0\) but generally \(y_j>0\), so its error \(y_j-r_j\) remains nonzero through the common probability normalization.

long.title: Audit one binary batch update and the resulting decision
long.source: PDF pp.31-37; new numerical application and cost-sensitive extension

parts.question: Train on \((x,r)=(-2,0),(1,1),(3,1)\), starting from slope \(w=0\) and intercept \(b=0\). Use summed cross-entropy and one batch gradient step with learning rate \(0.1\). Compute the gradients and new parameters.
parts.solution: All probabilities are \(1/2\). The intercept gradient is \(1/2-1/2-1/2=-1/2\). The slope gradient is \((1/2)(-2)+(-1/2)(1)+(-1/2)(3)=-3\). Hence \(b_{\rm new}=0.05\) and \(w_{\rm new}=0.3\).

parts.question: Compute the new probabilities and total cross-entropy. Compare it to the initial loss; exact logarithmic expressions are acceptable.
parts.solution: New logits are \((-0.55,0.35,0.95)\), with probabilities approximately \((0.3659,0.5866,0.7211)\). The loss is \[\log(1+e^{-0.55})+\log(1+e^{-0.35})+\log(1+e^{-0.95})\approx1.3158,\] below the initial \(3\log2\approx2.0794\). The first term uses label zero and a negative score; the other two use positive labels.

parts.question: Using the equal-cost threshold, classify all three training points. Does a zero classification error here imply that further loss reduction is impossible?
parts.solution: The first probability is below \(1/2\), and the other two are above it, so all three labels are correct. Positive correct-side logits can still increase in magnitude, raising correct-class probabilities and reducing cross-entropy; zero label error is not zero cross-entropy.

parts.question: Now suppose predicting \(C_1\) when the truth is \(C_2\) costs four, while the reverse error costs one, with zero correct-decision loss. Derive the posterior threshold and classify the same points under this cost rule.
parts.solution: Compare \(4(1-y)\) with \(y\): choose \(C_1\) only if \(y>4/5\). None of the three fitted probabilities exceeds \(0.8\), so all are assigned to \(C_2\). This changes the decision rule while retaining the same fitted probabilities.

long.title: Train a three-class model and check the normalization

parts.question: Consider one training sample \(x=(2,-1)^{\mathsf T}\) in class \(C_3\). Use augmented input \(\widetilde x=(1,2,-1)^{\mathsf T}\) and a row-weight matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}\), initially zero. Compute the one-hot target, probabilities, and loss.
parts.solution: The target is \(r=(0,0,1)^{\mathsf T}\), all logits are zero, probabilities are \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\), and cross-entropy is \(\log3\).

parts.question: Compute the full gradient matrix and update \(B\) using learning rate \(1/2\). Display every entry and state its dimension.
parts.solution: Each row is \((y_i-r_i)\widetilde x^{\mathsf T}\), so \[\nabla_B\ell=\begin{bmatrix}1/3&2/3&-1/3\\1/3&2/3&-1/3\\-2/3&-4/3&2/3\end{bmatrix},\qquad B_{\rm new}=\begin{bmatrix}-1/6&-1/3&1/6\\-1/6&-1/3&1/6\\1/3&2/3&-1/3\end{bmatrix}.\] Both are \(3\times3\). The signs are from subtracting one half of the gradient.

parts.question: Recompute the logits, the probability of \(C_3\), and the new loss at this sample. Identify the predicted class.
parts.solution: Multiplying each row by \(\widetilde x\) gives logits \((-1,-1,2)\). Thus \(y_3=e^3/(2+e^3)\approx0.9094\), each other probability is \(1/(2+e^3)\), and loss is \(\log(1+2e^{-3})\approx0.0949\). Class \(C_3\) wins.

parts.question: Add the row vector \((10,0,0)\) to each fitted row of \(B\). Prove whether probabilities change, and describe a numerically stable way to compute the original softmax.
parts.solution: The shared row adds ten to every logit, so all probabilities remain identical after cancellation. For stable evaluation, subtract the largest original logit, two, obtaining \((-3,-3,0)\), and normalize the exponentials \((e^{-3},e^{-3},1)\).
